analysis.one_liner: Makes the corporate research tax credit permanent and more generous, without paying for it.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 274-131 on May 9, 2014 with support from both parties, but the Senate never took a vote, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the federal research tax credit and made it permanent, with no expiration date. It raised the credit rate to 20% of qualifying research costs and added a credit for payments to energy research consortiums. It did not include any tax increase or spending cut to pay for the cost, and it specifically exempted itself from the statutory pay-as-you-go scorecard that is supposed to flag deficit-increasing legislation. The research credit had long been a temporary provision that Congress renewed every year or two; this bill would have locked it in permanently.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that spend heavily on research and development — pharmaceutical, biotech, technology, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing firms — would gain a larger, permanent tax credit, making their federal tax bill permanently lower and removing the uncertainty of annual expirations. Investors in those companies would benefit through higher after-tax returns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: R&D-heavy corporations like pharma and tech

how_it_helps.text: It gives companies a credit of 20% of qualified research expenses above 50% of their average for the prior three years, up from the roughly 14%-equivalent credit in existing law, a direct increase in the subsidy for research spending.
It repeals the credit's expiration date, so companies no longer face the risk that the credit lapses between congressional extensions — a stability the annual-expiring credit never offered.
It simplifies the credit's formula, which supporters argued would make the credit easier to claim and more effective at encouraging research hiring and investment.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally. The credit expansion was not offset by any tax increase or spending cut, and the bill exempted itself from the statutory pay-as-you-go scorecard, so its full cost would have added to the federal deficit and eventually been borne through future taxes, lower spending, or higher debt.

drawbacks.text: The bill was not paid for: it made a large tax credit permanent and prohibited its budgetary effects from being entered on either statutory PAYGO scorecard, meaning its cost would simply add to the deficit.

The credit mostly rewards research companies were already doing, since it applies to expenses above 50% of the prior three years' average — so much of its cost goes to existing researchers as a windfall rather than to new research that would not otherwise happen.

House Democrats offered a motion to recommit that would have conditioned the credit on equal pay for women, priority hiring of unemployed Americans and veterans, no outsourcing of jobs, and deficit neutrality; the House rejected it 191-209.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for making the research credit permanent: companies plan research over years, and the old annual expiration-and-extension cycle reduced the credit's incentive value. But this version carried serious costs. It increased the credit's generosity and made it permanent with no offset, and it explicitly removed the credit's cost from the statutory pay-as-you-go scorecard [S4][S5] — a step that protects the bill from the very rule meant to keep tax cuts and spending from adding to the deficit. Because most claimants already spend heavily on research, much of the credit pays companies for research they would have done anyway, so a large share of the cost is a windfall rather than new innovation. A stronger bill would have paired permanence with an offset.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 274-131 on May 9, 2014, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX) introduced the bill on April 9, 2014, to simplify and make permanent the research tax credit.
The Ways and Means Committee approved it on April 29, 2014, by a vote of 22-12, and reported it on May 2.
The rule for floor debate closed the bill to amendments, so the only vote besides passage was a Democratic motion to recommit.

On May 9, Democrats offered a motion to recommit that would have required credit claimants to guarantee equal pay for women, give priority to hiring unemployed Americans especially veterans, refrain from outsourcing jobs, and bar the bill from taking effect if it increased the deficit. It failed 191-209, with all but one Republican voting no.
The House passed the bill 274-131 on May 9, 2014. Nearly every Republican present (212 of 232) voted yes, and 62 of 199 Democrats joined them.
The Senate received the bill on May 12, 2014, and never took any action on it. It died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers came out ahead in the near term, because the deficit-financed, permanent expansion of the corporate research credit never became law; the existing credit continued under the usual annual-extension process.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the corporate tax cut died

sides.party_line_note: Passage was bipartisan in raw numbers — 274-131 with 62 Democrats joining 212 Republicans — but the parties split sharply: 91% of voting Republicans yes versus 31% of voting Democrats, and the Democrats' motion to recommit failed with all but one Republican opposed.

industries.note: Drug and biotech firms are among the largest claimants of the research credit, so a bigger, permanent credit permanently lowers their tax bill. The cost is carried by taxpayers through a larger deficit.

Software and technology firms claim the research credit heavily for product development and engineering wages. Permanence increases the value of the credit and removes the uncertainty of annual extensions.

Manufacturers with large engineering and product-development budgets gain from the higher 20% rate and permanence. Any public benefit from added research is diffuse, while the fiscal cost is concrete.
The bill adds a new 20% credit for corporate payments to energy research consortiums, a narrower benefit for companies funding cooperative energy research.
